name: Subdermal Armor Pigment
description: Introduces an ultra-dense melanin layer beneath the skin that functions as both UV shielding and mild impact resistance. The melanin is structured in layers similar to nacre (mother of pearl), creating a biological composite material that distributes impact force across a wider area. The protection is modest — it reduces bruising, prevents minor lacerations from blunt trauma, and provides SPF 200+ sun protection — but it's invisible and always on. The skin takes on a slightly deeper, richer tone from the additional melanin, which many users find attractive. Crucible Genomics offers the modification with optional patterning — the dense melanin areas can be shaped into designs visible only under specific lighting conditions, creating 'hidden' body art that reveals itself in UV light or under extreme sun exposure.
source_organism: Synthetic structured melanin construct, Haliotis rufescens (red abalone, nacre structure genes)
procedure: Dermal injection with melanin structuring retroviral carrier, 2 sessions
reversibility: Partially reversible with melanin suppression; skin tone changes persist
side_effects: Slightly reduced skin sensitivity from dense melanin layer
UV-reactive hidden patterns may reveal themselves at inconvenient times (tanning, certain lighting)
Rare: melanin overproduction creating visibly dark patches
social_perception: Subtle and well-regarded. The modification provides real protection without visible change. The richer skin tone is considered attractive by most. The hidden-pattern option is popular among people who want body art that's private until they choose to reveal it.
story_hooks: A murder victim's subdermal armor pigment patterns contain a message visible only under forensic UV examination — they wrote something in their own skin knowing they might die
A batch of War Paint from a Shelf clinic contains melanin that resonates at a specific electromagnetic frequency, making every recipient detectable by a proprietary scanner
